eez-shelf.essay:
The sea next to a coast is divided in law into belts, measured outward from a line called the baseline, usually the low-tide edge of the land. A nautical mile, the unit used at sea, is about 1.85 km. The first belt, out to 12 nautical miles, is the territorial sea, where the coastal country has nearly the same authority as on land. The next, reaching 200 nautical miles (about 370 km), is the exclusive economic zone, or EEZ. Under the water lies the continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast, which in some places runs further than 200 nautical miles.

These belts come from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Coastal countries wanted the fish, oil and minerals off their shores, and every country wanted ships and aircraft to keep moving. So the coastal country does not own the water outright. It holds rights to the resources (Articles 56 and 57), while others stay free to sail, fly and lay cables (Article 58), paying due attention to its rights. A public road across a farm works in a similar way. Anyone may travel the road, and only the farmer may plant crops or put up a barn. Shelf rights do not depend on occupying the seabed (Article 77), so a country that has never sent anyone there still holds them.

A Flanders Marine Institute poster using 2019 data counts 230 EEZs covering 136,850,878 km², leaving out joint arrangements and overlapping claims. Russia's is the largest at 7,734,809 km², followed by Australia's at 6,871,622 km². The US agency NOAA puts the US zone at more than 3.4 million square nautical miles.

The rule that decides nearly everything is Article 60, which Article 80 extends to the shelf. It gives the coastal country the exclusive right to build and authorize artificial islands, along with installations that have an economic purpose or could interfere with its rights. It also gives that country exclusive legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. Artificial islands are not islands in law, so they have no territorial sea of their own and change no sea boundary (Article 60(8)). Safety zones around them may reach 500 metres at most, unless international standards allow more (Article 60(4)-(5)). The country may also board and arrest to enforce its fishing rules (Article 73) and may chase a ship out to sea for violations in the zone, known as hot pursuit (Article 111).

Suppose a group anchors a platform 100 miles off Florida and declares it independent. The spot is inside the US EEZ, so the first question is whether the structure had US permission. If the group asks and gets it, the platform comes under US tax and immigration law, and the independence it wanted is gone. If it does not ask, the record offers comparisons. In 1970, in United States v. Ray, a US appeals court banned building on two reefs off Florida, holding that the country's exclusive rights over its shelf were enough even though it did not own the reefs. When a company proposed a nation called Taluga on Cortes Bank, about 111 miles off San Diego, the US government declared the bank US territory as part of its shelf.

One part of the law is unclear. UNCLOS does not define "artificial island", and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. A boat passing through is plainly using the freedom in Article 58. A structure that stays put and houses people for the long term looks more like what Article 60 covers, which appears to rule out an independent project unless the coastal country agrees. The coastal country has the boats on site, so its reading takes effect first and any court comes later.

The clearest real case is XLII, a six-metre-wide cabin on a weighted column in the Andaman Sea, built by a company called Ocean Builders. Its owners said it sat just over 12 nautical miles off Phuket, and other accounts say about 14. The American bitcoin trader Chad Elwartowski and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019, and he said 20 more would be sold. The Thai navy said they had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April. Thailand revoked his visa and charged them under a law carrying life in prison or death, saying they had endangered national sovereignty, and navy boats towed the cabin toward shore as evidence. Ocean Builders argued that the site was in the contiguous zone, the band 12 to 24 miles out where a country has limited powers, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its EEZ. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. How the case ended is not known, so no court is known to have decided whether Thailand's criminal law reached that far.

Even a real country gets no special treatment. In 2011 President Anote Tong of Kiribati, whose low-lying islands are threatened by rising seas, said his government was considering floating islands, at about $2 billion to come from other countries. He named no site, three years later his government bought land in Fiji, and no platform was built. Under Article 60(8), a platform would not by itself carry the sea rights that land generates.

If the structure counts as a ship, it needs a real country's flag, which brings that country's law on board (Articles 91 and 94). Ocean Builders' later cruise ship plan, the MS Satoshi, collapsed in 2020 because no insurer would provide the liability cover a ship's owners need. Payments between countries travel through banks that hold accounts with each other, and those banks need a supervisor they can rely on, which a platform lacks. One law journal puts a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million, and selling stakes to raise such money can count as selling investments. The US regulator sued the promoter of New Utopia over a $350 million bond offering that raised $24,000.

Tax follows the person. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, as the Supreme Court held in Cook v. Tait in 1924. Food, fuel and parts come through a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Ship captains must rescue people in danger at sea (Article 98), and a rescued person lands in some other country under its law, so serious medical care means going ashore. A birth, marriage or will on a platform would need a registry others accept, and without one a child's papers and an inheritance would appear to depend on the parents' home countries.

The commonest misunderstanding is that everything past 12 nautical miles is international waters. That is correct for passing ships and aircraft and wrong for resources and fixed structures. A second is that a declaration changes the zone. The usual test for a state, Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other countries, and a structure that is no island in law provides no territory.

The most workable version is an agreement with the coastal country carving out a special zone, which Article 60 lets it authorize. Honduras changed its constitution in 2013 to allow private zones such as Próspera, and its Supreme Court struck those laws down in 2024. French Polynesia signed a memorandum with the Seasteading Institute in 2017 and said in 2018 that it was void. Whatever freedom exists is a grant from one government that a later government can review.

territorial-sea.essay:
The territorial sea is the belt of water next to a coast. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a country may set it at up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km) from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured (Article 3). The normal baseline is the low-water line on the country's official charts (Article 5).

Inside this belt the coastal country has full authority over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as over its land (Article 2). It exercises this subject to UNCLOS and other international law (Article 2(3)). The main limit is innocent passage, the right of foreign ships to pass through peacefully and without delay (Articles 17 and 19). A private road that the owner must let travellers use is similar, since a traveller may drive through and may not stop and build a house. Staying put to set up a settlement appears to fall outside what passage covers, on a reading of Articles 18 and 19. Submarines must travel on the surface and show their flag here (Article 20).

A further belt reaches out to 24 nautical miles. In it the country may act to prevent and punish customs, tax, immigration and health offenses committed in its territory or territorial sea (Article 33).

The practical result is that a structure here is a domestic building project. Suppose a group anchors a platform 5 nautical miles off a coast and declares independence. The group is inside the country, in the same legal position as someone who puts up an unapproved building on land and announces that it is a new state. Harbour, building, tax and police officials all have ordinary powers. A nearby officer can visit, and the group's boats have to land at that country's docks.

Giorgio Rosa's Rose Island shows how little room there is even near the line. His 400-square-metre platform stood nearly 12 km off Rimini, a few hundred metres outside Italian waters as they were then measured. The Rimini harbour office asked him to stop in late 1966. He declared independence on 1 May 1968, and police and tax officers took control on 26 June, 56 days later. A project inside the limit would not even have the argument about position that Rosa made.

The line itself is less simple than it looks, and two British cases teach this. Roy Bates ran a pirate radio station on Knock John, a wartime fort about 16 km off Essex, where British broadcasting law could reach him only if the fort lay inside the three-mile limit then used. Distance is measured from a line set by law, which need not follow the shore. Magistrates fined him £100 in 1966, and his appeal failed when the court held that the fort lay on the landward side of that line. Radio 390, on Red Sands fort, lost in the High Court in December 1966, two judges to one, because the distance could be measured from a sandbank that shows only at low water. Neither fort had moved. A person therefore cannot judge the limit with a map and a ruler from the beach.

A country can also move the line. Bates went on to Roughs Tower, which he declared to be Sealand in 1967. The fort sits about 6 to 7 nautical miles off the English coast, or about 11 to 13 km, and at that time it was outside British waters. In 1987 the UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles, which put the fort in waters recognized as British. Offshore installations and artificial islands, for their part, do not count as harbour works and cannot push the boundary out in the builder's favour (Article 11). So the limit can grow toward a project, and a project cannot grow the limit.

Three real projects show what is possible when the country's law is accepted from the start. The Seasteading Institute of San Francisco chose French Polynesia, a self-governing French territory, for its calm lagoons. In January 2017 the territory's government signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. It opened the way to studies of "seazones" with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers. Residents objected and opposition politician Valentina Cross protested. On 28 February 2018 it was reported that the government considered the deal to have no legal force and to have expired at the end of 2017. Nothing was built. The government could walk away at no cost because nothing binding had been signed.

SeaPods came from Ocean Builders, the same company whose cabin off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy in 2019. It turned to homes at Linton Bay Marina in Panama, with $100 deposits and prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. Each home stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors. At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, the pump that clears water from a hull, and denied that it sank, and no injuries were reported. Guests were staying in one by June 2023. The company claims no independence, and the number of permanent residents is not known.

Oceanix Busan is the largest of the three. On 18 November 2021 the city of Busan in South Korea, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX agreed to build a prototype floating district, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost, and they unveiled the design at UN Headquarters in April 2022. At the developers' $10,000 per square metre, its 15.5 acres would come to about $627 million. A conference in October 2023 gave no concrete financing or construction plans, construction is not known to have started, and no one is known to live there. Building on the sea and leaving national law are separate things, and this project attempts only the first.

The ordinary bumps follow from being inside a country. Permits come first, and residents can stop them, as in French Polynesia. Ocean Builders' cruise ship plan outside national waters collapsed in 2020 when no insurer would give liability cover. Tax on residents stays as it was. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income, and the host country may tax local income too. Medical care, schooling, inheritance and birth records run through the country's normal systems, which is an advantage for families. Police and courts have the same reach as on the shore, so a dispute over a floating home would go to an ordinary local court.

The common misunderstandings come from treating water as different from land. A boat's flag does not take a settled home out of the coastal country's law, since passage rights do not cover staying. A declaration does not change the zone either. Stuart Hill, who declared a Shetland islet the state of Forvik in 2008, was still charged with motoring offences in a Scottish court. UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto and two-thirds of the General Assembly.

The most workable version is a licensed floating neighbourhood or marina, or at most a special zone written into the host country's law by its legislature. Calm water, short supply lines and a nearby hospital make building here among the easier options at sea, and holding out against the coastal country close to impossible. The limit is that any self-government lasts only as long as that country's politics allow, and a memorandum alone gives no protection.

reefs-low-tide-elevations.essay:
A reef is shallow and often far from any town, so founders have often chosen one as a place to start a country. The law treats it according to two facts, whether the feature stays dry at high tide and which legal zone of the sea it lies in.

The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, sorts features into three kinds. An island is naturally formed land, surrounded by water and above water at high tide (Article 121(1)). A rock is an island that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of its own. It gets a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water of up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 km), and no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf, the wider belts of resource and seabed rights (Article 121(3) and Article 3). A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water only at low tide. If it is more than 12 nautical miles from land, it has no territorial sea of its own (Article 13). Most reefs that founders have chosen fall into this last group.

In 2016 a panel of judges set up under UNCLOS, called the South China Sea tribunal, ruled on this. It found that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". It also held that a feature's status depends on its natural condition, before any building. It found that no feature in the Spratly Islands can generate an exclusive economic zone, and that they cannot do so collectively as a unit. So a low-tide reef cannot be claimed by moving onto it, and it belongs to whichever legal zone it lies in.

That rule closes the most natural idea, which is to dump sand until the reef stays dry. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, and an artificial island generates no territorial sea (Article 60(8)). Building is physically possible, as Minerva's founders showed in 1971 by barging sand from Australia. Safety zones of up to 500 metres are set by the coastal country and not by the builder (Article 60(4)-(5)). If the reef is inside a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt up to 200 nautical miles from its coast, that country must authorize the work (Article 60).

Suppose a group finds a reef 100 nautical miles from a country's coast and starts to build. The first question is whose zone it is in, and a reef that far out normally answers to that country. United States v. Ray shows what happens next. In the 1960s two rival groups, the Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold, planned countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, about four and a half miles off southeast Florida, in what were then international waters. The US Army Corps of Engineers refused a permit in 1964, and Louis Ray dredged anyway. A trial court barred building in 1969 and rejected a trespass claim, since the government did not own the reefs. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, where US law and the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the country exclusive rights to resources, and it ordered a full permanent ban, noting harm to corals and shipping.

The Republic of Minerva shows the other route, which is annexation, meaning a country formally adding the place to its territory. Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer, raised money from about 2,000 investors, and his group declared independence on the reefs between Fiji and Tonga on 19 January 1972. Tonga had not included them in its 1887 claim. At a conference on 24 February 1972, about five weeks later, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles on 15 June, and an expedition arrived on 18 June. The king came with a convict work party, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In 1982 a group led by Morris Davis, Minerva's former provisional president, tried again, and Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. Annexing the reef then left two states arguing. Fiji rejected Tonga's sea claims from the reefs in 2005, its navy destroyed navigation equipment there in 2010 and 2011, and the dispute is not known to have been settled.

Other projects ended earlier. Operation Atlantis, begun by the soap executive Werner Stiefel in 1968, lost a concrete boat to capsizing and then to a storm. At Silver Shoals, claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas, gunboats ordered his group away, and accounts differ on whose they were. Haiti cancelled a lease on Tortuga after officials read the group's newsletter, and a hurricane destroyed an oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank. Abalonia, planned in 1966 for Cortes Bank about 111 miles off San Diego, lost its anchor ship when waves broke it up on Bishop Rock. A later plan there, Taluga, was stopped when the US declared the bank part of its continental shelf. Leicester Hemingway's raft New Atlantis, 8 by 30 feet off Jamaica, relied on the US Guano Islands Act of 1856, was refused by the Universal Postal Union when it tried to sell stamps, and was destroyed by storms before any court tested it. Autopia, on the Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean, stalled for lack of money after a steel frame was built in 2002. Its founders called the site high seas, while Wikipedia says Mauritius administers the whole bank because part lies in its exclusive economic zone.

Money brings its own legal risk. New Utopia, planned for the Misteriosa Bank, was never built and existed as an offer of bonds at 9.5 percent. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission sued, a judge froze the money, and in January 2000 Lazarus Long, the promoter, accepted a final judgment. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised. Investors, insurers and banks all live in real countries, so their rules reach the project wherever its reef is.

Then come the physical problems. A low-tide reef has no fresh water and no soil, and storms have destroyed rafts, ships and rigs in the cases above. A reef also carries environmental duties. The South China Sea tribunal held that building land at seven reefs breached a country's duties on the marine environment. Serious medical care means a boat to someone else's port, and people there remain under their home countries' law, including US tax on worldwide income.

Two misunderstandings recur. One is that "international waters" means no one can stop a project. The shelf rules defeated this idea at Grand Capri and Cortes Bank. Another is that a reef beyond every country's zone would be free for the taking. The seabed there belongs to the deep ocean floor regime under UNCLOS, and Article 137 says no one may take any part of it as their own. A declaration of independence also does not supply the "defined territory" that the Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty defining a state, requires.

The most workable version is modest. A coastal country can license a research or reef restoration station on a reef in its zone, and the station then operates under that country's law. Another version is to give up the reef altogether. A participant in Operation Atlantis says the group later bought Hatchet Caye, an ordinary island in Belize, and lived there until 2005. A reef can offer a physical base for a while. It offers little legal protection, nearby states have repeatedly acted within months.

abandoned-platforms.essay:
Steel and concrete structures stand in open water off many coasts, and some are no longer in use. A disused platform already has a deck and legs and needs no dredging, so people have tried since the 1960s to use wartime sea forts and purpose-built platforms as bases for independent projects.

The first thing to understand is that an empty structure is not an ownerless one. Two separate kinds of right apply. One is ownership, which belongs to whichever company or government built or bought it, and entering without permission can be trespass. The other is legal power over the place, which belongs to a country. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an installation in a country's exclusive economic zone, the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles from its coast where it controls resources, stays under that country's sole legal power. The same applies on its continental shelf, the seabed extending out from the coast (Articles 60(2) and 80). Oil platforms stand on a shelf, so they normally fall under that power. Buying a platform from its owner would appear to transfer ownership only, because the country's legal power under Article 60 does not come with the sale.

The treaty also expects old structures to disappear. Article 60(3) says abandoned or disused installations must be removed to keep shipping safe, and any remains must be made public. The London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted. A platform has no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has, so it cannot be the base of a claim to the water around it (Article 60(8)). Installations are also not part of the coast when boundaries are drawn (Article 11).

Suppose a group boards a disused oil platform 50 miles off a coast and raises a flag. Boarding is physically possible. The owner, who may still be responsible for removing the platform, now has unauthorized people on its property. The coastal country has legal power over the structure, so its police or navy can come out. If anyone is hurt, or the structure fails, the questions of who pays would go to that country's courts.

Sealand is the case everyone cites,. Roughs Tower was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex. That was then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just lost a court case over Radio Essex on Knock John, another fort, because the court found that fort lay on the landward side of the legal line measuring the limit. He moved to Roughs Tower, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a buoy. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that the firearms law did not apply, because Parliament had never extended it beyond three miles. That ruling decided only how far a statute reached. In 1978 a Cologne court held that Sealand was no state. That August a German lawyer seized the fort, and the Bateses retook it by helicopter. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower, and it has left the place alone since. The Bates family says Britain and Germany have recognized it in practice, and neither government accepts this. Roy Bates died in 2012. Michael lives in England, the family sells titles and an online citizenship at about $10 a month, and one caretaker lives on the fort. Sealand's fort stood outside the limit when the claim began, and a new project would not have that history.

Other governments did not leave their forts alone. Sunk Head, about 18 km off Essex, stood clearly outside British waters too. When the law banning offshore broadcasting took effect in August 1967, Royal Engineers placed 3,200 pounds of explosives and blew it up on 21 August, leaving only stumps. Red Sands, home of Radio 390, lost in the High Court in 1966 on a measurement from a sandbank that shows only at low water, and it went off the air on 14 August 1967 under the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. In June 1966 men boarded Radio City's fort in a dispute over a transmitter, its owner Reginald Calvert was shot dead at the home of a rival, Oliver Smedley, and Smedley was cleared on grounds of self-defence. The killing turned public feeling against the stations, and enforcement rose.

REM Island was built for commercial radio and television about 10 km off Noordwijk and fixed to the seabed in cement. Broadcasts began in August 1964. On 12 December the Dutch government passed a law declaring the seabed under it Dutch territory, and marines boarded five days later. Rose Island, a 400-square-metre platform nearly 12 km off Rimini, declared independence on 1 May 1968. Italian police and tax officers took control on 26 June, 56 days later, and blockaded it. The navy set explosive charges twice in February 1969, the second time on 13 February, and a storm sank what remained on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the independence claims unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad.

Holding a fort leaves the other problems open. HavenCo was set up on Sealand in 2000 to keep customers' data beyond the reach of courts. Law professor James Grimmelmann found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family and could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim of independence. Operations stopped in 2008. Banks need a supervisor they can rely on, and a fort has none. Sealand's passports were revoked in 1997 after a Madrid-based ring sold fakes, and using such a document at a border may bring charges. Unauthorized broadcasting allows arrest by any country receiving the signal (Article 109). Old steel and concrete need upkeep, and a 2006 fire on Sealand sent one person to hospital, with damage estimates ranging from £100,000 to half a million pounds. People on board keep their home countries' tax duties, a rescue lands them in another country, and locking someone up on the platform appears able to count as unlawful detention elsewhere.

Common misunderstandings follow from Sealand's fame. The 1968 British ruling said a statute stopped at three miles and did not recognize Sealand. Occupying a structure gives no title to it, and buying one gives no country. The usual test for a state, in the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with others. Sealand has had one or two residents in recent years, and its territory is a deck that UNCLOS treats as no island.

The most workable version is an ordinary lease or purchase from the owner, with the coastal country's approval, for a business such as research or tourism, under that country's law and with a plan for eventual removal. REM Island's later life points the same way. The Dutch government used it to measure sea temperature and salt levels, and it has been a restaurant in Amsterdam's harbour since 2011. A new occupation claiming independence would have little legal basis on a shelf or in an exclusive economic zone, and most of its chance of lasting would depend on a government choosing not to act.

disputed-islands.essay:
A disputed island is land that more than one country says is its own. The best-known examples are the Spratly and Paracel Islands in the South China Sea. A place with several rival owners can look as if it has no owner, but each claimant holds that the land is already its own, and on the Spratlys and Paracels they keep armed garrisons. A newcomer would be one more claimant facing armed occupiers.

The land itself is small. The Spratlys have 177 hectares of natural island area, or about 200 hectares counting reclaimed land, in the table used by Wikipedia. That table also shows who occupies what. The Paracels are more than 30 islands, under Chinese control in practice since 1974. The value lies mostly in the water and seabed around them, because under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, land can generate rights over nearby sea.

Those rights depend on what kind of land it is. Article 121(3) says rocks that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of their own get no exclusive economic zone, the belt up to 200 nautical miles where a country controls resources, and no continental shelf, meaning seabed rights. In 2016 a tribunal, a panel of judges set up under Annex VII of UNCLOS, decided a case brought by the Philippines. The award, issued on 12 July 2016, found that no feature in the Spratlys can generate an exclusive economic zone, individually or as a group. It found no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources inside the nine-dash line, the line China uses for its claims in the sea. It also found that China's land-building at seven features caused severe harm to coral and violated its duties, and that China built on Mischief Reef inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone. The award is final and binding on the parties under Article 296. China took no part.

The tribunal ruled on sea zones and said it does not rule on any question of who holds authority over land territory. Who owns each island remains a matter between the claimant countries. Land-building creates no new territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that natural land has (Article 60(8)), and because a feature's legal status depends on its natural condition, engineering work gains no legal ground.

Two older rulings show how such disputes between countries have been decided. In the Island of Palmas case of 1928, the arbitrator Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, that being nearby gives nothing, and that continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title. In the Clipperton case of 1931, the arbitrator found that on an uninhabited island a state's clear intention and brief presence can be enough. Both rulings concern states competing with states, and the acts they describe are acts of government.

Suppose a group lands on an unoccupied sandbar in the Spratlys and raises its own flag. The first response would likely come from whichever country holds the nearest feature, and removing the group would need no court. No one has tried this recently, so the best guide is what happened to earlier claimants.

Tomás Cloma was a Filipino businessman with a fishing fleet and a maritime school. On 11 May 1956 his brother Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and they posted a Notice to the Whole World. Tomás argued the area had no owner because Japan had given it up in the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty, and he declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May. In October 1956 Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat at North Danger Reef, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. The brothers then asked the Philippine government for support. In 1972 President Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In December 1974 he was arrested and made to sign over his rights to the Philippines for one peso, and a 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan. The Philippines cites that transfer as one basis for its own title. So the private claim survived only as an asset of a state.

An older rival was the Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads, a claim made only in documents. Its supporters said a British captain, James George Meads, claimed the islands in 1877, and none of this has been shown to be true. The first checkable evidence comes from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, an American soldier, was discharged in Manila. His stories drew Cloma's attention. The group never set up a settlement, its requests for recognition in 1972 went nowhere, and its $25 billion lawsuit of 1985 was never heard.

In 1893 James Harden-Hickey proclaimed himself Prince of Trindade, an uninhabited South Atlantic island, and sold bonds. Britain took possession in 1895 for a telegraph station, Brazil won the dispute with Britain, and the Brazilian navy keeps a post there. The Kingdom of EnenKio claimed Wake Island, controlled by the United States since 1899 and also claimed by the Marshall Islands. The Marshall Islands government condemned it in 1998, and in October 2000 the US Securities and Exchange Commission won a court order freezing the assets of Robert Moore over $1 billion of unregistered Gold War Bonds. How that case ended is not known.

Rockall, a bare rock in the North Atlantic, shows the gentler response. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972, and Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it. Greenpeace landed in June 1997 to protest oil exploration, stayed 42 days and declared the Global State of Waveland. The British government answered that Rockall was British and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased. Treating the activists as ordinary visitors meant it never had to act. Tom McClean had earlier spent 40 days there in 1985 to strengthen the British claim, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. One person's stay does not settle whether a rock can support human habitation, the test in Article 121(3).

Everyday problems come after the military one. Supplies would come by boat from a port belonging to a claimant or a neighbour, and a serious injury would mean rescue into one of those countries. Building would raise the coral damage the tribunal condemned. A passport or stamp from such a place gets no recognition, and UN membership needs nine of 15 Security Council votes with no veto, on a council where China holds a permanent seat.

The most common misunderstanding is that a dispute creates a gap, when to each claimant a newcomer is an intruder on its own territory. Another is that a court win for one country, such as the 2016 award, opens the islands to others. It decided sea rights only.

A private person can realistically do two things here. One is to visit or work under the administration of whichever claimant holds a feature, accepting that country's rules and the risk that its rivals object. The other is a short protest occupation in the style of Waveland, whose value is publicity and which has no standing in any country's law. States with existing claims have little reason to accept a new one.

undersea-water-column.essay:
A habitat under the sea is hard to see, and some people expect it to be hard for the law to reach. In law, depth changes very little. The water and the sea floor follow the zone at the surface above them, and being underwater does not create a separate legal space.

The ocean has layers of law, under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. In the territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles from a coast, the coastal country has full authority over water and seabed, and submarines must travel on the surface and show a flag (Article 20). Further out, the seabed is usually a country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor extending from its coast. Article 77 gives that country exclusive rights to the shelf's resources, and Article 80 applies Article 60, so artificial islands, and installations with an economic purpose or that could interfere with its rights, need its permission. Further out still, the water above is high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, while the bottom is "the Area", the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). Article 137 bars anyone from taking any part of it. Article 147 applies ISA rules to installations used for mining, so it does not appear to clearly reach a habitat with no mining.

So a person must first ask whether the habitat moves. A moving craft would likely count as a vessel. High-seas freedoms apply to the water (Articles 86 and 87), so a submerged vessel under a flag appears to be treated as a ship, although UNCLOS does not define "ship". A flag means a real country's registration, and that country's law comes aboard. Without one, the rule in Article 110 on boarding a vessel with no flag still applies to a submarine, though a warship has to find it first. Hiding is a practical advantage only, and it ends at every port call.

A fixed habitat is the harder question. On a continental shelf it needs the coastal country's permission where Article 60 applies, and any anchor appears to give that country a physical point of contact. Research installations follow the rules of the zone where they sit, have no island status, and get safety zones of 500 metres at most (Articles 258 to 260). On the deep seabed, taking any part as your own is barred, and the ISA's rules on installations are written for mining. The treaty gives no clear answer on whether a stationary habitat tethered to the seabed counts as a ship or an installation, and the question appears open. The seafloor reaches more than 8 km deep in the Mariana Trench, according to the ISA, while the deepest habitat described below went to 610 feet off a coast.

To see why it stays shallow, it helps to understand saturation diving. Water pressure forces breathing gases into the body, and after long enough at depth the body reaches a steady state. Divers in that state can work outside for hours, and they need to decompress, returning slowly to surface pressure, only once at the end of the mission. They cannot simply swim up in an emergency. A sick person in a habitat therefore has a slow trip to any hospital.

The history starts with governments. Jacques Cousteau's Conshelf experiments put two divers 12 metres down off Marseille for two weeks in 1962, and in 1963 placed six people 10 metres down in the Red Sea off Sudan for 30 days. Air, water, food and power all came from a large team on the surface. Part of the money came from French petrochemical firms, and later work showed that robots and divers from the surface could do industrial jobs more efficiently, so companies lost the reason to pay for people on the bottom. The US Navy's SEALAB I went to 192 feet off Bermuda in 1964. SEALAB II followed in 1965 off California, where Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30 days. SEALAB III went to 610 feet in February 1969, 18 months late and $3 million over budget, and the aquanaut Berry Cannon died during a repair. A Navy inquiry found his breathing equipment lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, and a 2024 study by an ocean engineer pointed to electrocution. The programme was halted.

What has lasted operates under a coastal country. Aquarius sits 62 feet down, 5.4 miles off Key Largo in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government. Built in 1986 and placed there in 1993, it was owned by the US ocean agency NOAA, and Florida International University took over operations in 2013. Jules' Undersea Lodge, a former research laboratory, is in a lagoon at Key Largo with a dock and a gift shop, and it is a building under water to which state and federal law apply. DEEP, a private UK-based company, installed its prototype Vanguard at Tennessee Reef in the same sanctuary in June 2026, designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more, and it was working toward classification by DNV, a body that certifies marine equipment. Its planned Sentinel modules would hold six people each at 200 metres for 28 days. Because they can be moved, a different country's permission would apply at each site.

The plans further out have not been built. Proteus, proposed by Fabien Cousteau for a marine park off Curaçao with government backing, was reported to need US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for three years, and in October 2024 it was still in planning. Ocean Spiral, a 2014 design by Shimizu Corporation, described 5,000 people in linked spheres at ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion, and expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay. Aquatica, proposed by Dennis Chamberland, a former NASA bioengineer, spoke of children born under water with schools and hospitals. Its first step, a four-person house called Leviathan, is not known to have been placed, and the plan named no site or legal basis. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely lie on some country's shelf.

Suppose a family wanted to live on such a habitat beyond any permit. Surface boats would have to bring food, gas and spare parts from a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Children would need birth records and schooling from somewhere. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. Crime on board would come under the law of the flag country or of the people's own countries, since US law, for one, reaches any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation for offenses by or against US nationals.

The main misunderstanding is that depth brings legal shelter. Nothing in UNCLOS gives it. A second is that living on the bottom earns a claim to it. SEALAB, Conshelf and Aquarius all kept people on the sea floor for long periods and gained no rights to the seabed. A third is that a habitat is a territory for the purposes of statehood. Research installations have no island status, and the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for a state, asks for a defined territory and a permanent population. Staying long term also depends on supply from the surface.

The most workable version is the one that exists, a licensed habitat for research, training or tourism in a coastal country's waters, staffed in rotation and supplied from shore. Going deeper or further out adds cost and risk and brings no new legal shelter, and the habitat's position remains that of a licensed structure under the country above it.

deep-seabed-area.essay:
Beyond the continental shelves, the seabed that extends out from each country's coast, lies the deep ocean floor. By the International Seabed Authority's own figure, this area covers about 54% of the total area of the world's oceans. In law it is called "the Area". Nobody can own it.

The reason goes back to minerals. By the 1970s companies were preparing to collect manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps of metal on the deep floor, and no treaty said who could mine there. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the 1982 treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, answered by declaring the Area and its resources the "common heritage of mankind" (Article 136), meaning they belong to humanity as a whole. A shared fund run by one body for all its members works in a similar way, since no member may take a slice for itself.

Article 137 sets out the core rule. No country may claim authority over any part of the Area, no country or person may take any part of it as their own, and no such claim or taking will be recognized. Rights in the resources belong to humanity as a whole, and minerals can be sold only under the rules of the International Seabed Authority (ISA), based in Jamaica (Article 137(2)-(3)). The ISA is the body through which member countries control activities in the Area, and all UNCLOS members belong to it (Articles 156 and 157). It was set up on 16 November 1994. It had 172 members as of 6 February 2026, made up of 171 countries plus the European Union.

Other rules fill in the picture. The status of the water and air above stays the same (Article 135), so the water remains high seas, open ocean outside any country's control. The Area is open to use for peaceful purposes only (Article 141). Archaeological and historical objects found there are to be preserved or disposed of for the benefit of humanity (Article 149). Installations used for mineral activities must be placed and removed under ISA rules, and they "do not possess the status of islands", so they cannot have a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water (Article 147(2)).

To mine, an operator needs sponsorship from a member country and an approved plan of work (Article 153). A sponsor is a country that takes responsibility for the operator. This requirement closes the obvious route for a new state, since a self-declared country cannot sponsor itself. It is not a member, so it would have to find a real one willing to answer for it, and that puts the operation under that country's supervision.

Suppose a group sent down a submersible, placed a marker on the sea floor and announced a new country on it. A submersible visit needs no ISA permission if it is only a visit, because the ISA's control concerns mineral activities. The marker gives no title. Article 137 says the claim will not be recognized, so the group would hold a piece of equipment on the sea floor with no legal right to exclude others. If the group then started collecting nodules, it would be taking something that belongs to humanity as a whole, and anyone buying the metal would be dealing outside the ISA's rules.

Deepsea Ventures tried a careful version in 1974, before the treaty existed. This American company, of Gloucester Point, Virginia, wanted the nodules in a deposit of 60,000 square kilometres in the northeastern Pacific. On 15 November its president, John Flipse, sent a notice of discovery to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, asked for diplomatic protection, and recorded a copy at a local courthouse. It claimed exclusive rights to mine and sell, and it said it was claiming no territory. It promised production within 15 years. The 1982 treaty later put the area under the authority, mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it.

Today the working system is contracts. The ISA lists 15-year exploration contracts with 22 contractors. Its text counts 19 for nodules, 7 for sulphides and 5 for crusts, 31 in all, although its sulphide sub-count adds up to 8, so the page is not fully consistent. Most are in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico. Only exploration is allowed so far. The rules for exploitation, meaning commercial mining, known as the Mining Code, were still unfinished after the July 2026 session of the ISA Council. The March 2026 Council approved no commercial mining, with benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. In July the Council asked its staff for a roadmap and a new negotiating text, and the draft decision says commercial mining should not take place without rules.

The Metals Company shows the main challenge to this system. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011, and its subsidiaries hold ISA exploration contracts, NORI sponsored by Nauru and TOML sponsored by Tonga. In June 2021 Nauru told the ISA it meant to begin mining, which started a two-year deadline to finish the rules, and the rules were not finished. The US has not joined the UNCLOS deep-sea mining system. It has a rival route, the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the US agency NOAA to speed up permits under that law, and four days later the company's American arm applied. On 9 March 2026 NOAA found the application to be in "substantial compliance", and it published the application for comment in August 2026, with no permit issued by that month. The ISA's commission is investigating whether this breaches contractors' duties. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal ordered the ISA to respect fair procedure in the inquiry, without suspending it. Two days later the Council extended NORI's contract to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending. The main case is undecided. If this route succeeds, it would give mining rights under one country's law and no territory to anyone.

Ordinary diving cannot reach these depths, so every visit needs a specialised vessel and submersible, and the seafloor elsewhere reaches more than 8 km. Food, power and rescue would all come from the surface, and rescue ends in some other country's port. Nothing built here would have island status. Any investor offered shares in a seabed nation would be buying a claim that Article 137 says will not be recognized, and securities law has been used against offers of that kind on the shallower reefs.

Common misunderstandings come from the mining news. A mining contract is a licence for a set activity for a set period, and it gives no ownership of the seabed. A US permit, if issued, would not make the patch American. The ISA's installation rules do not clearly reach a habitat with no mining, and that gap gives no permission, since Article 137 still bars taking any part of the floor as one's own.

The most workable activity is to take part in the system. A company can seek a sponsoring member country and an exploration contract, or a research group can work from a flagged ship under its flag country's law. What it gains is a contract right to explore. It gains no land, no people under its own law and no legal basis for a state.

underground-subseabed.essay:
Some people expect that a place deep enough underground, or under the sea floor, must be out of reach of governments. Digging is one of the easier ways to build a large private space, and the law runs downward from the surface, so going down does not change which country a person is in.

The rule on land comes from an old saying. The Latin phrase cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos means "whoever owns the soil, it is theirs all the way to the sky and to the depths". It has been traced to the 13th-century Italian lawyer Accursius, and William Blackstone gave it its broad form in his Commentaries on the Laws of England in 1766. Modern law keeps a limited version. Below the ground, an owner holds rights to what is underneath, although in many places minerals beyond a set depth belong to the government, which often leases them out. The saying settles who owns a chamber under a plot of land. That owner still holds it under the law of the country it lies in, as the owner of a basement holds it under the same town's rules as the house above.

A country's authority also runs down. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a coastal country's authority reaches the seabed and the rock beneath it in its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast (Article 2). Past that belt, the continental shelf is the seabed and the rock beneath it, out to the edge of the continental margin, where the continent's underwater slope ends, or to 200 nautical miles (Article 76(1)). The coastal country alone may explore the shelf and take its resources, and nobody else may do so without its express consent, even if it never uses them (Article 77). Article 85 adds that the shelf rules do not limit a coastal country's right to exploit the rock below by tunnelling, however deep the water above. So the water over a shelf may be open to every ship while the rock beneath stays under the coastal country's control. A private mining shaft or tunnel there would need its consent. The deep ocean floor beyond the shelves is not part of this system and has its own rules against private claims.

Suppose someone buys a disused missile silo in Kansas and announces a sovereign republic in it. The silo part has been done. In 2008 Larry Hall bought an Atlas missile silo at Raven Ridge near Concordia for $300,000. It goes down 197 feet. He built Survival Condo, a bunker of 15 floors and 12 condominium units for up to 75 people, with a pool, gardens, three years of stored food, armouries and a jail cell, at about $20 million by 2012. All of it remained ordinary property. Peter Ziegler, who bought a unit in 2013 and lent the company $3 million, died in 2017, and his estate sued in January 2019, saying assets had been moved to other companies. The two sides settled that August. Debts, lawsuits and courts reached the bunker as they reach any other property in Kansas, and a declaration of independence would not change which courts have power there.

The buyer's first bumps are the same as for any building. A bunker has an address, so officials can simply enter it. Ordinary police, fire and licensing law apply. Geology comes next. Vivos, a California shelter company, planned a site for 5,000 people in a former mine of 2,700,000 square feet at Atchison, Kansas, and cancelled it in June 2014 after Army geologists raised concerns about collapses. Its plan for a Soviet-built complex at Rothenstein in Germany was expected to need sprinklers throughout under fire rules. It lists 575 bunkers of about 2,150 square feet each at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota. Its membership figures, about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers in 2022, come from the company. Then there is daily use. Survival Condo had no owners living there in 2020, and a bunker's owner still needs electricity, water, food deliveries, schools and hospitals from above.

CyberBunker is the case of someone who did call it a republic. In 1995 Herman-Johan Xennt bought a former NATO bunker of 20,000 square feet at Kloetinge in the Netherlands, built in 1955 to survive a nuclear attack. His web-hosting business took any website except those with child abuse material or terrorism. Its spokesman, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, called it the Republic of CyberBunker and styled himself a minister. In 2002 a fire exposed a laboratory making the drug MDMA, three men were jailed, and the town refused a business licence. The servers moved above ground while the firm kept advertising the bunker. A Hamburg court barred it from hosting The Pirate Bay in 2010, and Kamphuis was arrested in Spain in 2013 over an attack on the anti-spam group Spamhaus. That year the firm bought a second bunker at Traben-Trarbach in Germany. Investigators tapped its traffic under a warrant from 2015 and sent in undercover officers posing as a gardener and a cleaner. In September 2019, 600 police raided it. In late 2021 the court in Trier convicted all eight defendants of belonging to a criminal organisation, though not of aiding their customers' crimes, with sentences of up to five years and nine months. Germany's Federal Court of Justice largely upheld the verdict in 2023. Warrants, wiretaps and undercover work all operated as they would against any business.

Pionen, a data centre in central Stockholm, makes no such claim. It occupies a 1943 wartime shelter of 1,100 square metres under 30 metres of granite, behind a door 40 centimetres thick, and the internet provider Bahnhof opened it on 11 September 2008. WikiLeaks kept servers there in 2010. It has a street address, and Swedish law applies as to any other business. A hardened site protects servers from physical harm, and its legal protection comes entirely from the law of the country it stands in. HavenCo on the sea fort Sealand sold a similar home for data and relied on a claim of independence, and that business stopped in 2008.

The remaining pitfalls follow from staying in one's own country. Taxes stay. The US taxes citizens on worldwide income in any case,. Internet addresses come from regional registries through a real legal entity. Passports issued by a bunker republic are not recognized, and using one at a border may bring charges. Children attend ordinary schools and inherit under the ordinary law, and a will or a mortgage works as usual.

The main misunderstanding is that depth is distance from the country. Rock under a shelf already has a holder by treaty, so tunnelling under the sea floor does not reach a free zone. Owning land also does not include the right to set its law.

The most workable version is what these businesses already are, a private bunker, data centre or shelter under local law with its permits in order. Buying the land is the easy part. Such a place can give physical security and some privacy. It does not change which country a person is in or protect against a lawful order.

inland-waters.essay:
An island in a lake or river can seem to sit between countries, especially on a border. The water around it belongs to the countries on its shores, and a newcomer gets no share. The ocean has a stretch that belongs to no one, the high seas. Lakes and rivers have nothing equivalent, because land under some country's control encloses them.

To understand how these borders work, start with a river. When two countries agree that a river is their border, they usually sign a treaty. A treaty that names only the river normally means the line follows the thalweg, the deepest channel, since that is the part boats use. Rivers shift and split, though, so the treaty may fail to say which channel it meant. Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 km² in the Chobe River that floods for several months each year. An 1890 treaty between Germany and Britain put the line in the "main channel" without saying which one. In 1996 Botswana and Namibia asked the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, to decide. In 1999 it studied the river and held that the northern channel was the main one, so the island fell on the Botswana side. Nobody lives there permanently, and it is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area. The case asked only which of the two countries held the island.

Lakes work the same way, with lines drawn by treaty or by old colonial orders. Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 m² in Lake Victoria, valued for the Nile perch in the waters around it. A colonial order, the Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council of 1926, draws the Kenya-Uganda line across the lake by straight lines between named islands, and it is copied into the Ugandan constitution. Two Kenyan fishermen say they settled the rock in 1991, a Ugandan fisherman says he arrived in 2004, and Kenya says Ugandan marine police raised a flag in June 2004. In February 2009 Kenyans there were told to buy special Ugandan permits. By then the rock held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino, with 131 people reported, while Ugandan police estimated about 500. Ministers agreed that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers, and they stayed. A 2009 survey placed the rock 510 metres on the Kenyan side, and its report was still unpublished in January 2025. Wikipedia says the results were announced and Uganda withdrew, while a Kenya News Agency report says surveyors disagreed and the joint work stopped. In January 2025 residents petitioned Kenya's president over harassment by Ugandan police, and that August fishermen said Ugandan officials were still seizing their gear. Settling first or raising a flag did not decide the matter.

Some waters have no agreed line at all. Lake Constance, where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet, has no binding agreement fixing the borders in its deep part. Areas under 25 metres deep go to the nearest country, and shipping and fishing have treaties of their own. Switzerland holds that the line runs down the middle. Austria says the deep part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement called a condominium, meaning shared rule. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous. Under every one of those views, the deep water belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so an outsider has no claim.

The Caspian Sea, at 389,000 km², is the largest case. Its five shore countries argued for decades over whether it counts as a sea or a lake, because the law of the sea applies only to seas. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea was signed on 12 August 2018 at Aktau, Kazakhstan. It would give each shore country 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water and a further 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface would be a common space open to the five members, and the seabed is left to agreements between the countries concerned. It was not in force as of September 2026, because all five must ratify it, meaning formally approve it. Four have. Iran's cabinet approved it on 22 July 2026 and sent it to parliament, which had not ratified it. Even the open middle is for the five named countries, so an outsider has none of the freedoms found on the ocean. Iranian patrol boats have at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed oil fields.

A treaty can also give an island to two countries at once. Pheasant Island, in the Bidasoa river, stays a condominium of France and Spain under the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659, and each governs it for six months in turn. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres. It is uninhabited and eroding, and access is forbidden apart from rare heritage days. Naval personnel check it every five days.

A river island can also be overlooked for a time. Ada Kaleh, in the Danube, was forgotten at the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and stayed Ottoman in law, with other countries on both banks. Its residents paid no tax or customs and were not drafted, and it became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest. Austria-Hungary declared sovereignty in 1913, Romania occupied it in 1919, and the Treaty of Lausanne, which the residents did not sign, made it Romanian in 1923. In 1970 the Iron Gates dam flooded it. Ada Kaleh had a legal owner throughout, and its residents had no say in the treaty or the dam.

New land raises a fresher problem. Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, with about 3,000 people under Peruvian administration. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made it a district of its Loreto region. Colombia's president said in August that Peru had "appropriated it by law". Colombia argues that the island had not formed when the 1922 and 1929 treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. Peru treats it as an extension of an older island. Land that a river newly creates may fall outside a treaty's words, and the competition for it still runs between the neighbouring countries.

Suppose a group floats a platform onto a large lake and declares a state. Lake police and customs officers from the nearest shore are a short boat ride away, and they are the practical limit. Every supply run ends at a dock in one of the shore countries. There is no high-seas freedom to argue from. Banks, tax, courts and building permits are those of the shore country.

The common misunderstanding treats a gap in a line as a gap in ownership. A border argument, a missing treaty, a shifting channel and a forgotten island have each been resolved or left open among the countries on the shore.

The most workable version is ordinary. A floating home, lodge or tourist concession can be built on lakes and rivers with the permission of the country that holds the spot, under that country's law. Building is easier than at sea, and supply and medical care are close. It gives no new status, since it is one more property in an existing country, and on a contested border it may bring officials from two countries, as on Migingo.

terra-nullius-land.essay:
Nearly all the dry land on Earth is claimed by some country. A few small pieces appear not to be, and the two most famous are Bir Tawil, between Egypt and Sudan, and Gornja Siga, on the Danube between Croatia and Serbia. Some people conclude that they can go there, plant a flag and start a country. That idea rests on an old legal term.

Terra nullius is Latin for land belonging to no one. In international law it is a technical term for how countries acquire land. The International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, described it in its Western Sahara opinion of 1975 as land that can be acquired by occupation (paragraph 79). Occupation in this classic sense is something countries do, so an individual's flag appears not to be enough on a reading of that passage. Two older rulings show what was expected. In the Island of Palmas case of 1928, Max Huber held that discovery gives only a starting claim, and that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title. In the Clipperton case of 1931, the arbitrator held that on a completely uninhabited island a state's clear intention, public notice and brief presence could be enough. Those rulings describe governments competing, and Western Sahara added a limit. The practice of countries at the relevant time did not treat land inhabited by tribes or peoples with social and political organization as terra nullius, and the Court applied that to Western Sahara's nomadic peoples (paragraphs 80 and 81).

Bir Tawil exists because of two lines drawn under British control, a straight political line of 1899 and an irregular administrative line of 1902. Egypt relies on the first and Sudan on the second, because each line gives that country the more valuable Halaib Triangle. Under either position Bir Tawil, 2,060 km² of desert, belongs to the other, so neither claims it. It has no water source and can be reached only through Egypt or Sudan. People also use it, including the Ababda people, according to a paper cited by Wikipedia, and migrants from Sudan dig for gold there. Under the Western Sahara reasoning, that use weakens any description of the land as empty.

On 16 June 2014 Jeremiah Heaton, a Virginia farmer, planted a flag there and declared the Kingdom of North Sudan so that his daughter could be a princess. He said he asked permission in Cairo for the trip, he applied for UN observer status, and he offered titles for $25. Suyash Dixit of India drove in on 4 November 2017 and declared the Kingdom of Dixit, and others announced a Kingdom of Middle Earth and a Kingdom of the Yellow Mountain. These rival private claimants have no court to settle anything between them, because only states can hold title to territory in international law. No one has settled there and no government recognizes any of them.

Gornja Siga is about 7 km² of forest and floodplain. The border was drawn by a 1947 commission whose conclusions were never made law, according to the Italian newspaper Il Post. Serbia places it on the river's deepest channel, and Croatia uses old land records following the river's earlier course. Both countries treat this as a border dispute, which is different from giving the land up, so whether it belongs to no one is contested. Croatia controls access on the ground. On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka declared the Free Republic of Liberland there, and it attracted hundreds of thousands of citizenship applications, according to Vice. Croatian police have detained and fined people entering, and one was sentenced to 15 days in prison. In August 2023 supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September, and on 21 September a private company removed the camp under police watch. The Free Republic of Verdis, on a neighbouring 128-acre strip, tried a camp in October 2023. Its founder says Croatia destroyed it within days and banned him permanently. The Kingdom of Enclava was declared in 2015 by a Polish tourist on a plot between Slovenia and Croatia, after he read online that it was unclaimed. Slovenia's foreign ministry said the plot was part of a claim going to international arbitration. Even the Sapodilla Cayes, a small uninhabited atoll run by Belize, are in a case at the International Court of Justice, with Honduras and Guatemala involved.

Suppose a person tries Gornja Siga. The first bump is the border, since reaching it means crossing Croatian or Serbian controls. Croatia says visitors must obey Croatian law, so the person faces detention, a fine and possibly an entry ban. At Bir Tawil, the first bump is passing through Egypt or Sudan, then water, food and fuel carried from there. The next bumps are the same at both sites. Banks need a recognized supervisor and treaties run only between states. A passport from such a place is a novelty that may bring charges if used at a border. US citizens still owe tax on worldwide income. Children's birth records and any inheritance would run through the parents' home countries. Verdis reported about 15,000 applications at $16 each, and Liberland reported about 6,000 paying e-residents.

History does contain self-governing places in such gaps, and they lasted only while their neighbours tolerated them. Cospaia, created in 1440 by a treaty that named a creek when two creeks had the same name, held about 250 people. Florence and the Papal States accepted it in 1484 because that was cheaper than redrawing the line, and their successors divided it in 1826. Couto Misto, three villages on the Spain-Portugal border, paid tax to neither until the Treaty of Lisbon of 1864. Neutral Moresnet, 3.5 km² around a zinc mine, was set up by the Netherlands and Prussia in 1816 and run by their commissioners, grew from 256 to 4,668 people, and ended with Germany's annexation in 1915. Bottleneck, a strip left by an error on Allied occupation maps, ran itself with 17,000 people from 1919 to 1920 until Germany returned. Kowloon Walled City held about 33,000 people on 2.6 hectares because Britain and China each declined to act, and they demolished it once they agreed to.

Other gaps closed by force. Indian Stream, settlers in land claimed by both the US and Britain, declared independence in 1832 to stop paying tax twice, and New Hampshire's militia ended it in 1835. No Man's Land, the present Oklahoma panhandle, had thousands of settlers and a government called Cimarron Territory, and Congress refused to recognize it and joined the strip to Oklahoma Territory in 1890. Jonathan Lambert declared himself ruler of Tristan da Cunha in 1810 or 1811, drowned in 1812, and Britain took the islands in 1816 by sending a garrison.

A common misunderstanding concerns Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist. It says a state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others, and Article 1 still requires a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states. In its Kosovo opinion of 2010 (paragraph 84) the Court found that general international law contains no applicable ban on declarations of independence. That is a narrow point, and the Court did not say that a declaration creates a state.

A claim can operate as an online community, a publicity project or a legal experiment, with its members living elsewhere, as Liberland's do on houseboats and in a village on the Serbian side. Permanent settlement has not been achieved at either site. The older cases suggest that a lasting arrangement would need the neighbouring countries' agreement, which none of Egypt, Sudan, Croatia or Serbia has offered.
